summary: A builder can start the Node.js + Mongoose sample now. All runtime and read-only verification tools the sample needs are present (node/npx, Azure CLI sign-in, the documentdb MCP server, and Microsoft Learn search). Several cold-answer facts were incorrect or outdated (notably resource type, CLI group, billing model, auth options, connection-string shape, and vector/index syntax) and must be corrected before coding; the agent kit skills installed plus the learn docs supply the corrections. Missing developer conveniences (mongosh on PATH, azd/bicep/terraform) and a few unspecified sample decisions (seed-data shape, Mongoose pin) are the remaining gaps but do not block the build.
summary_points: Ready to start: Node (v24), npx, az (signed in), documentdb MCP server and the Microsoft Learn documentation server are available and sufficient to implement and verify the sample against the live cluster.

Major cold-answer corrections are required: the cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts), the Azure CLI group is az documentdb mongocluster (not az cosmosdb), billing is vCore/compute-tier (vCores) for this service (not RU-based), and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) is supported alongside native SCRAM auth.

DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire versions 5.0–8.0; vector indexes (IVF, HNSW, DiskANN) and built-in BM25 full-text search (`createSearchIndexes` + `$search`) are supported — the exact syntax differs from community MongoDB and must be copied from the Microsoft docs.
Installed documentdb-* agent skills cover driver patterns, connection tuning, indexing, vector search and local gateway usage and are available as the primary agent guidance.

Missing but non-blocking developer tools: mongosh is not on PATH (useful for interactive checks); azd, bicep and terraform are not present but not required for this sample's live-cluster verification.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for a database account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters use the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider and the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for vCore clusters; Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts is the Cosmos DB database account resource (different product/resource shape).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (Bicep/ARM/Template reference)
Microsoft.DocumentDB databaseAccounts (ARM template reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and historical reuse of the 'DocumentDB' / 'Cosmos DB' names caused conflation between the vCore-managed Mongo cluster resource and the older Cosmos DB databaseAccounts resource.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses databaseAccounts in ARM/Bicep or az cosmosdb commands, they will create or manage a Cosmos DB account (RU-based) rather than the vCore Mongo cluster resource; deployment templates, CLI calls and resource ids would be wrong.
improvements: Document: Add a bolded note on the 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts' and 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' pages explicitly distinguishing the two services and their use-cases.
Agent kit: Add a quick-check snippet that warns when a template uses databaseAccounts for vCore clusters and suggests mongoClusters instead (documentdb-azure-deployment skill).

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create: az cosmosdb create --name <account> --resource-group <rg> --locations regionName=<region> --default-consistency-level Session. This is in the core Azure CLI (no separate extension required for basic create/manage operations).
confusions.grounded_answer: The CLI group to manage vCore DocumentDB clusters is az documentdb mongocluster (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create / show / list / update); these commands are provided in the Azure CLI command group documented under 'az documentdb'.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster (az CLI docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB CLI group (az cosmosdb) manages Cosmos DB databaseAccounts; a new/specialized az documentdb group manages the vCore mongoClusters resource, so the names and CLI groups are easily confused.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands will produce Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) resources or the wrong CLI flows; the script or README would direct users to incorrect CLI invocations.
improvements: Azure CLI docs: Add a cross-link and short note on az cosmosdb pages: 'If you mean vCore-managed Mongo clusters (DocumentDB), use az documentdb mongocluster.'
Agent kit: Provide sample az documentdb mongocluster CLI snippets in the deployment skill.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account.
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB Mongo clusters the Bicep/ARM resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (various API versions). Terraform deployments typically use AzAPI or Azure Verified Modules (avm-res-documentdb-mongocluster) targeting Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters rather than azurerm_cosmosdb_account.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/TF reference)
AVM Terraform module for Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB account resource and the newer mongoClusters resource share the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider; past patterns for Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) differ from the new vCore cluster resource.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts or azurerm_cosmosdb_account in IaC will create the wrong resource type (Cosmos DB RU-mode account) and not the vCore mongoClusters cluster, causing deployment templates and resource IDs to mismatch the sample's live cluster.
improvements: Bicep/ARM templates docs: Add a 'Which resource to use' section clearly showing when to use mongoClusters vs databaseAccounts and examples for common IaC flows.
Agent kit: Provide a Terraform/AzAPI example that creates Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and references the AVM module.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical form: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. You can also use mongodb+srv:// if the account supports SRV; otherwise use explicit host + port 10255 and include ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, and retryWrites=false.
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB clusters the preferred connection strings use the mongodb+srv scheme and hostnames in the *.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com domain (or *.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com for global endpoints). Drivers should use TLS (tls=true or tls/ssl set appropriately); recommended options include retryWrites=false and setting the auth mechanism appropriately (SCRAM-SHA-256 for native auth or MONGODB-OIDC for Microsoft Entra ID). The legacy Cosmos DB RU endpoints and port 10255 are a different product shape.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB (connection examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflects the older Cosmos DB Mongo (RU) connection patterns (host suffix / port 10255) rather than the vCore cluster SRV hostnames and mongodb+srv pattern used by DocumentDB (mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com).

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB connection examples (older Cosmos docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix/port or missing SRV/TLS/AAD settings will cause connection failures or misconfigured auth (e.g., trying to use SCRAM where OIDC is required) and cause the sample to fail at runtime.
improvements: Quickstart: Add an explicit, prominent sample connection string for the two common modes (native SCRAM password and Microsoft Entra ID / OIDC) on the same page: quickstart-nodejs-mongoose.
Agent kit: Provide a one-line Mongoose connection snippet that sets recommended driver options (tls, retryWrites=false, serverSelectionTimeoutMS) for DocumentDB.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB is billed primarily on Request Units (RUs) for provisioned throughput ... dedicated vCore-based clusters exist in specific SKUs/offers.
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB service (the target here) capacity is provisioned by compute tier (vCore-style tiers such as M30, M40, etc.) and storage. The RU-based Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) billing model (Request Units) is a different offering (Cosmos DB RU-based / serverless accounts).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI (shows --tier like M30)
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (pricing/compute model)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both services are in the DocumentDB/Cosmos DB family and earlier Cosmos DB accounts used RU billing; the vCore offering uses explicit compute tiers that resemble vCore pricing rather than RU-based throughput.

confusion_sources.title: az documentdb mongocluster create CLI options (shows --tier M30 etc.)

confusions.build_risk: Assuming RUs would lead the builder to design throughput-dependent features (throttling, RU cost estimates) incorrectly; the cost and scaling guidance would be wrong for the target cluster.
improvements: Docs: Add a short 'Billing and capacity model' comparison table on the top of both the mongoClusters and databaseAccounts pages clarifying when RUs apply vs vCore tiers.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Mongo-compatible API authenticates with Mongo credentials (username/password / SCRAM). AAD integration exists for other Cosmos DB APIs but not as a native MongoDB wire-protocol auth method.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both native (SCRAM) username/password authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC token) authentication for the Mongo-compatible endpoints. Drivers can use OIDC via the MONGODB-OIDC auth mechanism and the connection string or driver parameters include authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC; the docs show how to configure the driver and obtain access tokens (DefaultAzureCredential patterns) for Entra ID authentication.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
az documentdb mongocluster create (auth-allowed-modes includes MicrosoftEntraID)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflected an assumption about Cosmos DB's older Mongo API limitations; the vCore DocumentDB product explicitly supports Microsoft Entra ID / OIDC for Mongo connections.
confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumes AAD isn't supported, they may implement only password-based secrets and miss implementing recommended, passwordless Entra integration for production.
improvements: Quickstart and Mongoose tutorial: add an explicit example showing MONGODB-OIDC connection string and code sample with DefaultAzureCredential so builders can copy it.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., mongodb Node.js driver) or higher-level ODMs like Mongoose for Node.js. There is no separate Mongo-specific Azure SDK for application data access; treat the service as a MongoDB endpoint and use the official Mongo drivers/ODM.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — use the standard MongoDB drivers (mongodb for Node) and high-level ODMs like Mongoose. Microsoft provides quickstarts and guidance using Mongoose and the mongodb driver for DocumentDB; there is no special proprietary SDK for application data access (the management plane uses Azure ARM SDKs separately).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB
Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Expect vector index support like MongoDB 7+ syntax: db.collection.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', vector: { dims: 1536, similarity: 'cosine', algorithm: 'hnsw' } }). Unsure about exact option names for this Azure variant.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports several vector index kinds with documented options: vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, and vector-diskann (DiskANN). Index creation uses a DocumentDB-specific index creation payload (cosmosSearchOptions / createIndex/createIndexes variants) documented in the vector-search docs; syntax differs from community MongoDB examples. DiskANN supports large dims and product quantization; IVF/HNSW have algorithm-specific params (numLists, m, efConstruction, etc.). Use the vector-search docs for exact payloads.

grounding_links.title: Vector search in Azure DocumentDB (DiskANN, HNSW, IVF and examples)
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (create index examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer guessed at community MongoDB 7+ 'vector' index syntax; DocumentDB exposes vector indexing but with its own create-index payload and option names (cosmosSearchOptions, kinds 'vector-ivf|vector-hnsw|vector-diskann').
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses the community MongoDB 7+ createIndex payload, index creation will fail; vector queries would not run until using the DocumentDB-specific index creation payload.
improvements: Add a short example on the vector-search landing page showing the exact create-index payload for each 'kind' and a one-line JS example that calls db.runCommand or the driver equivalent.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Options: (1) Use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ field: 'text' })). (2) For richer full-text or hybrid vector+text search, index Cosmos DB content into Azure Cognitive Search and use it.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB offers a built-in BM25 full-text engine exposed through createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage (BM25, fuzzy, phrase, custom analyzers). Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) is supported server-side by creating a BM25 search index plus a vector index and combining the ranked lists (Reciprocal Rank Fusion or server-side unionWith pipelines). You do not need an external Azure Cognitive Search index for rich hybrid searches.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes and $search)
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed either simple Mongo text indexes or external search services because earlier Cosmos DB patterns used external Azure Cognitive Search; DocumentDB now includes its own richer BM25 engine and hybrid capabilities.

confusion_sources.title: Manage indexing in Azure DocumentDB (text index docs showing db.createIndex text path as community style)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder opts to replicate data into Azure Cognitive Search unnecessarily, they increase cost and complexity and miss the simpler integrated $search + vector path.
improvements: Docs: Add a short 'when to use external Azure Cognitive Search vs built-in $search' comparison on the full-text landing page.
Agent kit: Provide a hybrid-search example combining $search (BM25) and cosmosSearch vector queries for RRF fusion.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically 3.6/4.0/4.2/4.4 and more recently 5.0/6.0 and newer; many managed accounts now support 6.x (and some offer 7.0 compatibility). Some features are limited (server-side JavaScript, certain admin commands, GridFS edge cases, some aggregation stages/transaction semantics may be restricted).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and documents feature compatibility tables. Some administrative commands and PaaS-managed operations remain different; check the compatibility matrix for exact operator and command support.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB FAQ (MongoDB wire protocol versions supported)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was imprecise and conservative; the authoritative docs explicitly list supported protocol versions (now including 8.0) and a feature-by-feature compatibility reference.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes an older Mongo version is enforced they might avoid language/features the cluster supports (or vice versa, attempt to use unsupported admin commands).
improvements: Compatibility docs: Add a top-line 'supported wire protocol versions' box on the compatibility page and call out major unsupported admin commands explicitly.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use a local MongoDB server (docker run mongo:7.0) on port 27017; the Cosmos emulator doesn't fully emulate the Mongo wire-protocol so use real Mongo or the live cluster.
confusions.grounded_answer: The project provides a DocumentDB local gateway docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes the gateway on port 10260 by default and includes options for TLS and SCRAM. You can run the local DocumentDB gateway (recommended by the DocumentDB local-deployment guidance) or use the live cluster for verification. The Cosmos emulator does not emulate Mongo API; using the DocumentDB local image or live cluster is the correct path.

grounding_links.title: Start DocumentDB in a Docker container (development loop)
Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB (note about local gateway port 10260)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer defaulted to 'use Mongo' since many teams run an official Mongo image locally; DocumentDB provides its own local gateway image optimized for DocumentDB compatibility and port 10260.
confusions.build_risk: If a builder runs plain mongo:7.0 locally without DocumentDB local image, subtle differences in behaviour or features (vector search / DocumentDB-specific preview features) may not appear in local testing.
improvements: Local-dev docs: Make the local gateway Docker command and default port 10260 very prominent on the quickstart and local-deployment pages.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are available on recent Mongo-compatible versions in managed offerings, but support can depend on the account SKU/version. Alternatively Cosmos DB exposes its own Change Feed. For Mongo change streams you typically need a replica-set-capable account and a server version that advertises change stream support; no special extra toggle beyond using a compatible account.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB change streams. For multishard clusters or certain scenarios you may need to enable a preview feature (Change streams for multishard clusters) from the cluster Features page; the docs describe enabling the feature when required. Cosmos DB also provides a separate Change Feed for other APIs, but for Mongo drivers use the Mongo change streams feature.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Mongoose on Azure DocumentDB (notes about Model.watch and enabling change stream preview for multishard)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged; the authoritative docs clarify that change streams are supported but multishard scenarios may require enabling a preview feature in cluster Settings.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are always on, they might be surprised by missing events on multishard clusters until the feature is enabled; the seed and verification steps relying on change streams could fail.
improvements: Add a checklist on the change-streams page: 'When to enable preview feature' with CLI/portal steps and expected behaviour changes.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (the prompt references a 'documentdb' MCP server). The general Azure MCP server covers generic ARM/control operations, but Mongo-specific data-plane inspection and tooling are provided by the documentdb MCP server/agent set.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane tools (find, aggregate, list indexes, explain, etc.). The general Azure MCP server handles control-plane and general Azure operations but not the fine-grained DocumentDB data-plane queries.
confusions.grounding_source: machine inventory (documentdb MCP server list) and installed skills

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name of Microsoft's document database service; it later evolved/was rebranded into Azure Cosmos DB (multi-model). The 'DocumentDB' name historically referred to that Microsoft service and is distinct from any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB. The Cosmos DB Mongo-compatible API is an API surface on top of the Cosmos DB engine providing Mongo wire-protocol compatibility.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is a source of repeated confusion: the *original* Azure DocumentDB (2014–2017) became Azure Cosmos DB. Separately, the vCore-based offering that used to be called 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' has been renamed to 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' — and this new DocumentDB is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine. So there are (at least) two different historical uses of the 'DocumentDB' name; the current vCore product is distinct from Cosmos DB RU-mode and from Amazon DocumentDB.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (naming and history)
Azure DocumentDB release notes (notes on rename from vCore Cosmos DB for MongoDB to Azure DocumentDB)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared names and multiple rebrands: 'DocumentDB' historically referred to the pre-Cosmos DB product (now Cosmos), and more recently the 'vCore' Mongo offering was rebranded 'Azure DocumentDB', causing mixing between the two histories.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder follows older 'DocumentDB' docs that actually describe the pre-2017 service or Cosmos DB RU-mode, they will use the wrong APIs or deployment resources.
improvements: Docs: Add a short 'Naming timeline' blurb on the top of the overview and FAQ explaining the two historically distinct uses of 'DocumentDB' and giving clear guidance which resource types and CLI groups correspond to the current vCore product.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath the Mongo-compatible endpoint is the Cosmos DB storage/engine (not a stock MongoDB server). The Mongo driver talks the Mongo wire protocol and Cosmos translates calls into its engine semantics. Application code using standard Mongo drivers and basic CRUD/aggregation patterns will mostly work, but there are semantic differences and feature gaps (transactions, certain commands, performance characteristics) you must validate against the managed engine.
confusions.grounded_answer: The vCore Azure DocumentDB service is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (governed by the Linux Foundation) — not on the Cosmos DB RU engine. Applications use the MongoDB wire protocol and official drivers; most CRUD and aggregation operations work but you should consult the DocumentDB compatibility matrices for any edge cases. The underlying engine is DocumentDB (open-source), and that is the material difference from Cosmos DB RU-mode or MongoDB server.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (engine and naming)
Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas (engine and portability)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed the underlying Cosmos DB engine; in fact the vCore offering is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (different from Cosmos DB's internal engine), which has implications for migration choices and licensing.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming the Cosmos DB RU engine behavior could lead to incorrect assumptions about features or performance tuning; consult compatibility docs before adopting advanced Mongo server-specific features.
improvements: Overview: Add a short, visible note that the vCore product runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine and list practical implications (licenses, supported features) for app authors.

confusions.question: What database name should this sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_customer_360_01 for everything the sample creates.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use database sample_customer_360_01 (this is explicitly required by the sample run-environment).

grounding_links.title: sample run-environment (skill_md)

confusions.question: Which environment variable contains the connection string and how should the app read it?
confusions.cold_answer: The connection string is provided in the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI. Read it at runtime (e.g., in Node.js: const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI) and do not hard-code the value in any file or logs.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run-environment instructs the builder to read the cluster connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime and never commit or log the secret.

grounding_links.title: sample run-environment (skill_md)

confusions.question: Which Node.js client and connection options should the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Mongoose (backed by the official mongodb driver). Example connection code: await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates: false, retryWrites: false, replicaSet: 'globaldb' });
confusions.grounded_answer: Use Mongoose (recommended quickstart). Connection examples in Microsoft docs prefer mongodb+srv hostnames, TLS enabled (tls=true), retryWrites=false in many examples, and either SCRAM credentials or MONGODB-OIDC when using Microsoft Entra ID. The quickstart shows Mongoose 9 and the bundled driver; follow the quickstart's connection snippet and driver options rather than a speculative option set.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB (shows connection pattern and recommends retryWrites=false example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed a generic mongoose option pattern with DocumentDB specifics; use the docs' concrete quickstart snippet for exact option names and the preferred SRV/TLS/AAD options.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong driver options (e.g., missing tls or wrong replicaSet) can cause connection failures or insecure behavior.
improvements: Quickstart: Add a single canonical Mongoose connect snippet (password + OIDC variants) that builders can copy verbatim into samples.

confusions.question: What index definition does this sample need for identity resolution?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a unique index on customerId to allow fast upserts: db.customers.createIndex({ customerId: 1 }, { unique: true, name: 'idx_unique_customerId' }).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the sample should create a unique index on customerId (e.g., { customerId: 1 } unique true) so upserts by customerId are efficient and atomic when used with upsert/updateOne patterns. Verify index creation via the documentdb MCP server or the quickstart examples.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Mongoose with Azure DocumentDB (index guidance and unique index examples)

confusions.question: What update pattern will the sample use to merge source-specific attributes without overwriting unrelated fields?
confusions.cold_answer: Use an upsert with $set targeted to a source-specific sub-document. Example Mongoose-style update: await Customer.updateOne( { customerId }, { $set: { [`sources.${sourceKey}`]: sourcePayload, updatedAt: new Date() }, $setOnInsert: { createdAt: new Date() } }, { upsert: true } );
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct and documented: use targeted $set to write only the source-specific subdocument (e.g., sources.crm) and $setOnInsert for createdAt. Use updateOne with upsert=true. The Microsoft quickstarts and driver guidance recommend reusing a single connection pool and using such targeted $set upserts for merge semantics.

grounding_links.title: Mongoose & Azure DocumentDB patterns (upsert $set examples in quickstarts)

information_gaps.title: Preferred Mongoose version for Node 24
information_gaps.description: Microsoft quickstarts recommend Mongoose 9 in many examples; there is no explicit official guidance for Node.js 24 compatibility beyond Mongoose compatibility tables. The builder should choose a concrete Mongoose version (e.g., latest Mongoose 9.x tested with Node 24) and document it in package.json. I checked the quickstart and Mongoose compatibility pages but didn't find a Node 24-specific pin.

information_gaps.title: Seed dataset shape and size
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks for sample data to verify upserts and queries but provides no required size or exact sample schema beyond crm/ecommerce/support sub-documents. No skill prescribes a canonical seed shape for a Customer-360 sample; developer must invent it. I scanned the quickstarts and local-deployment docs for guidance but found only examples, not a canonical seed.

information_gaps.title: Exact recommended driver retry and timeout values for production
information_gaps.description: The docs show examples using retryWrites=false in quickstarts, and advise testing; a single one-line canonical recommended value set for production-grade Node.js apps on DocumentDB (pool sizes, maxIdleTimeMS, serverSelectionTimeoutMS, retryWrites) was not found. The documentdb-driver and documentdb-connection skills offer guidance but no single production default set for Node 24/Mongoose 9 against an M30 cluster.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) when referring to or authoring IaC or ARM/Bicep for the vCore-managed DocumentDB cluster.
Use the az documentdb mongocluster CLI group for cluster management (az documentdb mongocluster create/show/list/etc.), not az cosmosdb when you intend to manage a vCore DocumentDB cluster.

Connect using the SRV mongodb+srv hostnames in the *.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com domain (or the global host) with TLS enabled; set options per the quickstart (e.g., tls=true, retryWrites=false where the quickstart uses it) and choose authMechanism SCRAM-SHA-256 for native credentials or MONGODB-OIDC for Microsoft Entra ID.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: For vector and full-text features, copy index creation and query syntax from the DocumentDB vector-search and full-text search docs (use cosmosSearchOptions, createSearchIndexes and the $search/cosmosSearch pipeline) rather than community Mongo 'vector' key syntax.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh on PATH for interactive checks and to run quick connectivity/index checks against the cluster (useful for manual verification). Example install: follow 'Install MongoDB Shell (mongosh)' on Microsoft Learn or install via the platform package manager; the quickstarts show how to use mongosh to verify connectivity.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this Node.js sample; the builder can use az / manual CLI / Bicep or the provided cluster. If IaC-driven app deploy pipelines are desired later, install azd per project needs.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for verification against the provided live cluster. Add if the sample intends to include full IaC provisioning automation; otherwise document how to apply an ARM/Bicep template via az deployment group create.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for sample coding and verification; add only if the builder will demonstrate IaC with Terraform. If needed, the agent kit docs and AVM module references show how to use AzAPI/AVM modules for mongoClusters.
